title: Is the NDIS Worker Orientation Module mandatory, and what does the NDIS Code of Conduct require of workers?
seoTitle: NDIS Code of Conduct and orientation
description: What the NDIS Code of Conduct requires of every worker, the 250 penalty unit civil penalty, and when the Worker Orientation Module is mandatory or expected.
shortAnswer: The NDIS Code of Conduct binds every NDIS provider, registered or not, and every person they employ or engage, including key personnel, contractors and volunteers. Breach is a civil penalty provision carrying up to 250 penalty units, or 10,000 for a serious contravention by a provider. The Worker Orientation Module 'Quality, safety and you' is mandatory for staff of registered providers through the Practice Standards, and recommended for all other workers.
keyTakeaways: Section 6 of the NDIS (Code of Conduct) Rules 2018 sets seven conduct duties plus a fair pricing rule added from December 19, 2023.
The Code applies through section 73V of the NDIS Act; individual workers face civil penalties of up to 250 penalty units, and the Commissioner can ban a worker under section 73ZN.
Completing the orientation module is a Practice Standards quality indicator for registered providers; for unregistered providers and their workers it is recommended, not required.
NDIS Commission guidance asks registered providers to build the module into induction and encourage existing workers to complete it over time.
The Commission's worker training portal has been offline since October 22, 2026; the Commission says it is preparing a simplified version of the module on its website.
appliesTo: Registered and unregistered NDIS providers and their key personnel
Employees, contractors, agents and volunteers engaged by NDIS providers
Providers of information, linkages and capacity building (ILC) activities
Providers of Commonwealth Continuity of Support Programme services for people over 65

sections.heading: What does the NDIS Code of Conduct require?

blocks.text: The Code requires anyone delivering NDIS supports to meet seven standards of conduct and not to overcharge participants for goods without reasonable justification. It is set out in section 6 of the [National Disability Insurance Scheme (Code of Conduct) Rules 2018](https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2018L00629/latest/text), which commenced on July 1, 2018 and were last amended by the Code of Conduct Amendment (2023 Measures No. 1) Rules 2023, in effect from December 19, 2023. This page states the position as at November 2026.
Under section 6(1), in providing supports or services to people with disability, a code-covered person must:

items: act with respect for individual rights to freedom of expression, self-determination and decision-making in accordance with applicable laws and conventions;
respect the privacy of people with disability;
provide supports and services in a safe and competent manner, with care and skill;
act with integrity, honesty and transparency;
promptly take steps to raise and act on concerns about matters that may impact the quality and safety of supports and services;
take all reasonable steps to prevent and respond to all forms of violence against, and exploitation, neglect and abuse of, people with disability; and
take all reasonable steps to prevent and respond to sexual misconduct.

blocks.text: Section 6(2), inserted in 2023, adds the fair pricing duty: a code-covered person must not, without a reasonable justification, represent or charge a higher price for goods supplied to a participant than for the same or substantially the same goods supplied to a person who is not a participant. The NDIS Commission describes pricing as fair when there is no major difference between the price for a participant and the price for other customers ([NDIS Code of Conduct](https://www.ndiscommission.gov.au/rules-and-standards/ndis-code-conduct)).

sections.heading: Who must follow the NDIS Code of Conduct?

blocks.text: Every NDIS provider and every person employed or otherwise engaged by one, plus key personnel. Section 5 of the Code Rules calls these 'code-covered persons' and makes no distinction between registered and unregistered providers. The NDIS Commission lists registered and unregistered providers, their key personnel and workers, ILC activity providers, and Commonwealth Continuity of Support Programme providers for people over 65.

The Commission's [Code of Conduct guidance for workers](https://www.ndiscommission.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-10/Code-of-Conduct-Worker-Guidance.pdf) (April 2024) states that 'workers' includes employees, contractors, agents and volunteers, and that a CEO or manager is also a worker if employed or engaged. When applying the Code, the Commission considers the type of supports, the organizational environment, the worker's skills and qualifications, and the participant's needs.

Victoria applies the same wording to every disability worker in the state, whatever the funding source, under the Disability Service Safeguards Code of Conduct (see [Victorian disability worker registration and standards](/regulations/victoria-disability-worker-registration-and-standards)).

sections.heading: What happens if a worker breaches the Code?

blocks.text: A breach is a contravention of section 73V of the [National Disability Insurance Scheme Act 2013](https://www.legislation.gov.au/C2013A00020/latest/text), a civil penalty provision. The penalty is 10,000 penalty units for a serious contravention by an NDIS provider and 250 penalty units in any other case, which includes individual workers. Section 73ZN(2) separately lets the Commissioner make a banning order prohibiting or restricting a current or former worker or key personnel member from specified activities, for example where the Commissioner reasonably believes the person has contravened the Act or is not suitable to be involved in providing supports.

Most responses are lighter. The worker guidance says that for less serious breaches the Commission may use training and education, warnings and directions; a matter may be referred to a professional body, may trigger reassessment of an NDIS worker screening clearance, or may go to police, while the most serious breaches can lead to court proceedings for civil penalties or a banning order. The Commission may also publish the outcome. Because a breach can affect a clearance, Code compliance and [NDIS worker screening](/regulations/ndis-worker-screening-requirements) should be managed in the same worker file.

The guidance also protects workers. It says workers directed to deliver supports they lack the training, competence or qualifications for should decline, and can report the direction to the Commission, with whistleblower protections available in some circumstances.

sections.heading: When is the Worker Orientation Module mandatory, and when is it only expected?

blocks.text: It is mandatory for staff of registered NDIS providers and recommended for everyone else. The obligation is not in the Code Rules themselves; it comes from the NDIS Practice Standards quality indicators that registered providers are audited against, and from how the NDIS Commission describes the module. The sources use slightly different words, so the table separates what is stated as mandatory from what is stated as expected.

blocks.text: Two practical points follow. First, the Practice Standards make completion an induction outcome for registered providers but do not set a renewal interval, so any refresher cycle is the provider's decision. Second, for unregistered providers the module is a sensible way to evidence the Code's 'safe and competent manner' duty, but its absence is not itself a breach. The [core and verification module context](/regulations/ndis-practice-standards-worker-training) explains the other induction and refresher indicators.

blocks.title: Training portal outage since October 22, 2026
blocks.text: The NDIS Commission states that its worker training portal was taken offline on October 22, 2026 as a precaution after a PHP software vulnerability affecting several government websites, that this affects workers trying to complete the Worker Orientation Module, and that it is working toward a simplified version of the module on its website ([worker training portal notice](https://www.ndiscommission.gov.au/workforce/online-training-modules/ndis-commission-worker-training-portal)). Providers onboarding staff during the outage should record the reason a certificate is missing and schedule completion once access returns.

sections.heading: How should a provider build Code of Conduct training and evidence?

blocks.text: Map each Code element to an observable behavior and a piece of evidence. The orientation certificate shows a worker has seen the Code; it does not show they apply it in the provider's setting. The Commission's guidance says providers and key personnel should check that their policies, procedures and training reflect the Code, and its [Training for Capability guidance](https://www.ndiscommission.gov.au/workforce/training-workers/guide-for-ndis-providers/training-your-workers) ties the 'safe and competent manner' duty to identifying learning needs and evaluating training.

blocks.text: The 'raise and act on concerns' and 'prevent and respond' elements connect directly to the duty of workers to report incidents, set out in [NDIS incident management and reportable incidents](/regulations/ndis-incident-management-and-reportable-incidents-training). A shared [training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) keeps the Code, orientation and incident training aligned by role.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry represents each paragraph of section 6 as a distinct obligation with its own learning outcome and assessment point, and records whether a requirement is legally mandatory, an audited quality indicator, or guidance. That distinction lets a provider answer the question an auditor or investigator actually asks: which duty was this training meant to evidence.

faqs.q: Do volunteers have to follow the NDIS Code of Conduct?
faqs.a: Yes. The Code applies to persons employed or otherwise engaged by NDIS providers, and the NDIS Commission's worker guidance states that workers include employees, contractors, agents and volunteers. A volunteer who breaches the Code can face the same responses as a paid worker, including education, a banning order or civil penalty proceedings.

faqs.q: How often must the Worker Orientation Module be repeated?
faqs.a: No interval is set. The Practice Standards treat completion as part of induction for registered providers, and the Commission asks providers to encourage existing workers to complete it over time. Providers can set their own refresher cycle, for example after a significant change to the Code or the module.

faqs.q: Does completing the orientation module satisfy all NDIS training requirements?
faqs.a: No. It addresses the Code of Conduct. Registered providers must also meet other Practice Standards indicators, such as infection prevention and control training, a system that identifies mandatory training and evaluates its effectiveness, and incident management training, plus any supplementary module requirements for the supports they deliver.

faqs.q: Does the fair pricing rule apply to support workers?
faqs.a: It applies to every code-covered person, but in practice it bites on whoever represents or charges a price for goods supplied to a participant. Section 6(2) prohibits a higher price for a participant than for a non-participant for the same or substantially the same goods without reasonable justification, so staff who quote or invoice goods need to know the rule.
